notes.front: What are imperative commands, in kubectl?
notes.back: Commands built into kubectl that create, update and delete live objects directly, without a configuration file.
notes.explanation: The docs stress speed: objects can quickly be created, updated and deleted this way, straight from kubectl.
notes.example: Typing kubectl create namespace dev at the prompt, rather than writing a Namespace manifest and applying it.
notes.evidence: Kubernetes objects can quickly be created, updated, and deleted directly using imperative commands built into the kubectl command-line tool.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”

notes.front: Which verb-driven kubectl command creates a new Pod to run a container?
notes.explanation: It is named so that users who do not know the Kubernetes object types can still recognise it.
notes.evidence: The commands are named to be recognizable to users unfamiliar with the Kubernetes object types. run : Create a new Pod to run a Container.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to create objects”

notes.front: Which verb-driven kubectl command creates a new Service to load balance traffic across Pods?
notes.explanation: It is one of the verb-driven creation commands, which cover some of the most common object types.
notes.evidence: The kubectl tool supports verb-driven commands for creating some of the most common object types. The commands are named to be recognizable to users unfamiliar with the Kubernetes object types. run : Create a new Pod to run a Container. expose : Create a new Service object to load balance traffic across Pods.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to create objects”

notes.front: Which verb-driven kubectl command creates an autoscaler that horizontally scales a controller such as a Deployment?
notes.explanation: The new autoscaler object does the scaling automatically; the controller it targets is what grows or shrinks.
notes.evidence: autoscale : Create a new Autoscaler object to automatically horizontally scale a controller, such as a Deployment.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to create objects”

notes.front: You need one throwaway Pod named probe, running busybox:1.28, with no controller behind it. Which command fits?
notes.choices:
A) kubectl run probe --image=busybox:1.28
B) kubectl create deployment probe --image=busybox:1.28
C) kubectl expose pod probe
notes.choicesExplained: B: this creates a Deployment, a controller that manages Pods. C: expose creates a Service for existing Pods; it starts no Pod.
notes.explanation: kubectl run creates a new Pod directly to run a container.
notes.evidence: run : Create a new Pod to run a Container. expose : Create a new Service object to load balance traffic across Pods.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to create objects”

notes.front: Which of these is an imperative command, rather than imperative or declarative object configuration?
notes.choices:
A) kubectl label pods web tier=front
B) kubectl apply -f web.yaml
C) kubectl create -f web.yaml
notes.choicesExplained: B: apply manages objects through files, which is declarative object configuration. C: create -f works from a configuration file, which is imperative object configuration.
notes.explanation: kubectl supports three kinds of object management, and only imperative commands work without a configuration file.
notes.evidence: The kubectl tool supports three kinds of object management: Imperative commands Imperative object configuration Declarative object configuration
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “Trade-offs”

notes.front: The type-driven creation command has the form kubectl create {{c1::<objecttype> [<subtype>] <instancename>}}.
notes.explanation: A subtype narrows the object: a Service, for example, can be created as a ClusterIP, LoadBalancer or NodePort Service.
notes.evidence: create <objecttype> [<subtype>] <instancename> Some objects types have subtypes that you can specify in the create command. For example, the Service object has several subtypes including ClusterIP, LoadBalancer, and NodePort.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to create objects”

notes.front: How do you list the arguments and flags that a kubectl create subcommand, such as create service nodeport, supports?
notes.back: Add the -h flag, e.g. kubectl create service nodeport -h.
notes.explanation: create service nodeport is itself a subcommand of create service, and -h shows what that subcommand supports.
notes.evidence: In the preceding example, the create service nodeport command is called a subcommand of the create service command. You can use the -h flag to find the arguments and flags supported by a subcommand: kubectl create service nodeport -h
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to create objects”

notes.front: Which kubectl create subcommand makes a Role with a single rule?
notes.explanation: The reference limits it to a single rule, so the Role it makes grants one set of permissions.
notes.evidence: kubectl create role - Create a role with single rule
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl create”, “See Also”

notes.front: Which kubectl create subcommand binds a Role or a ClusterRole to subjects within a namespace?
notes.explanation: The reference describes it as creating a role binding for a particular role or cluster role.
notes.evidence: kubectl create rolebinding - Create a role binding for a particular role or cluster role
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl create”, “See Also”

notes.front: Which kubectl create subcommand requests a token for a ServiceAccount?
notes.explanation: The reference describes it as a request for a token, not as creating an object.
notes.evidence: kubectl create token - Request a service account token
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl create”, “See Also”

notes.front: What can `kubectl create configmap` build a ConfigMap from?
notes.back: A local file, a directory or a literal value.
notes.explanation: The `kubectl create` reference lists exactly these three inputs for the `configmap` subcommand, so you can build one without writing a manifest.
notes.evidence: kubectl create configmap - Create a config map from a local file, directory or literal value
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl create”, “See Also”

notes.front: Which flag gives kubectl create cronjob its timetable?
notes.explanation: The Quick Reference example creates a CronJob that prints “Hello World” every minute with that schedule.
notes.evidence: create a CronJob that prints "Hello World" every minute kubectl create cronjob hello --image = busybox:1.28 --schedule = "*/1 * * * *" -- echo "Hello World"
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Creating objects”

notes.front: In kubectl create job hello --image=busybox:1.28 -- echo "Hello World", what does the part after -- give?
notes.back: The command the Job’s container runs.
notes.explanation: That is why the Quick Reference describes it as a Job which prints “Hello World”.
notes.evidence: create a Job which prints "Hello World" kubectl create job hello --image = busybox:1.28 -- echo "Hello World"
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Creating objects”

notes.front: You must give a team’s ServiceAccount the permissions of an existing ClusterRole, but only inside their namespace. Which command fits?
notes.back: kubectl create rolebinding, naming the ClusterRole.
notes.choices:
A) kubectl create rolebinding
B) kubectl create clusterrolebinding
C) kubectl create role
notes.choicesExplained: B: a cluster role binding grants the role across the whole cluster, not one namespace. C: this creates a new Role; it binds nothing to the ServiceAccount.
notes.explanation: The reference says a role binding can be made for a particular role or for a cluster role.
notes.evidence: kubectl create rolebinding - Create a role binding for a particular role or cluster role
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl create”, “See Also”

notes.front: Which command starts a single nginx Pod in the namespace mynamespace?
notes.explanation: kubectl run creates one Pod; -n sets the namespace for that single request.
notes.evidence: kubectl run nginx --image = nginx -n mynamespace # Start a single instance of nginx pod in the namespace of mynamespace
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Interacting with running Pods”

notes.front: What does --dry-run=client do to a kubectl create command?
notes.back: It only prints the object that would be sent; nothing is sent to the API server.
notes.explanation: Nothing reaches the cluster, so the command only shows you the object it would have sent.
notes.evidence: If client strategy, only print the object that would be sent, without sending it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl create”, “Options”

notes.front: --dry-run=server against --dry-run=client: what does the server strategy do differently?
notes.back: It submits a server-side request but does not persist the resource; client never sends it.
notes.explanation: The flag accepts none, server or client, and none is the default.
notes.evidence: Default: "none" Must be "none", "server", or "client". If client strategy, only print the object that would be sent, without sending it. If server strategy, submit server-side request without persisting the resource.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl create”, “Options”

notes.front: Complete the command that writes a Pod spec to a file without creating the Pod: kubectl run nginx --image=nginx {{c1::--dry-run=client -o yaml}} > pod.yaml
notes.explanation: The dry run stops the Pod being created, and -o yaml prints its spec so the shell can redirect it into pod.yaml.
notes.evidence: kubectl run nginx --image = nginx --dry-run = client -o yaml > pod.yaml # Generate spec for running pod nginx and write it into a file called pod.yaml
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Interacting with running Pods”

notes.front: A task asks for a Deployment with a field that kubectl create deployment has no flag for. What is the quickest start?
notes.back: Generate the manifest with --dry-run=client -o yaml, add the field, then create from the file.
notes.choices:
A) kubectl create deployment … --dry-run=client -o yaml > d.yaml, edit, then create
B) kubectl create deployment …, then delete and recreate it until it matches
C) Write the whole manifest by hand from memory
notes.choicesExplained: B: creating the real object first and retrying is slower and leaves live objects behind. C: works, but gives up the generated skeleton and invites typing mistakes.
notes.explanation: Printing the configuration as YAML instead of sending it gives you a file to edit before anything is created.
notes.evidence: The kubectl create service -o yaml --dry-run=client command creates the configuration for the Service, but prints it to stdout as YAML instead of sending it to the Kubernetes API server.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “Using set commands to modify objects before creation”

notes.front: Which kubectl command gets the documentation for Pod manifests from the command line?
notes.explanation: It answers questions about a manifest’s fields from the terminal.
notes.evidence: kubectl explain pods # get the documentation for pod manifests
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Creating objects”

notes.front: Editing a Pod manifest, you cannot remember which fields a Pod spec accepts. Which command answers this in the terminal?
notes.choices:
A) kubectl explain pods
B) kubectl describe pods
C) kubectl api-resources
notes.choicesExplained: B: describe prints detailed information about existing objects, not the fields a manifest may hold. C: api-resources lists resource types, not their fields.
notes.explanation: The Quick Reference lists explain as the command that gets the documentation for Pod manifests.
notes.evidence: kubectl explain pods # get the documentation for pod manifests
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Creating objects”

notes.front: What does kubectl api-resources show for each resource type?
notes.back: Its short names, API group, whether it is namespaced, and its kind.
notes.explanation: It lists every resource type the cluster supports, so it answers “what is this called and where does it live”.
notes.evidence: List all supported resource types along with their shortnames, API group , whether they are namespaced , and kind : kubectl api-resources
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Resource types”

notes.front: Complete the command that lists only non-namespaced resources: kubectl api-resources {{c1::--namespaced=false}}
notes.explanation: Setting the flag to true lists the namespaced resources instead.
notes.evidence: kubectl api-resources --namespaced = true # All namespaced resources kubectl api-resources --namespaced = false # All non-namespaced resources
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Resource types”

notes.front: You need the short name and API group of NetworkPolicy before writing a command. Which command gives both?
notes.choices:
A) kubectl api-resources
B) kubectl explain networkpolicy --recursive
C) kubectl get networkpolicy -o wide
notes.choicesExplained: B: explain documents fields; it is not the listing of short names. C: get lists existing NetworkPolicy objects, not facts about the type.
notes.explanation: The api-resources listing includes each type’s short names and API group.
notes.evidence: List all supported resource types along with their shortnames, API group , whether they are namespaced , and kind : kubectl api-resources
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Resource types”

notes.front: Which command permanently sets the namespace for all later kubectl commands in the current context?
notes.explanation: The namespace is saved in the kubeconfig context, so it persists across commands until changed.
notes.evidence: permanently save the namespace for all subsequent kubectl commands in that context. kubectl config set-context --current --namespace = ggckad-s2
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Kubectl context and configuration”

notes.front: Which command switches the default context to my-cluster-name?
notes.explanation: kubectl config current-context then displays the context now in use.
notes.evidence: kubectl config current-context # display the current-context kubectl config use-context my-cluster-name # set the default context to my-cluster-name
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Kubectl context and configuration”

notes.front: Every command in a task must run in namespace billing, and you keep forgetting -n. What saves the most typing?
notes.choices:
A) kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=billing
B) kubectl config use-context billing
C) kubectl create namespace billing
notes.choicesExplained: B: use-context switches to a context named billing, which probably does not exist. C: this creates a namespace; it does not change where commands run.
notes.explanation: The namespace is saved in the current context and applies to all later kubectl commands in it.
notes.evidence: permanently save the namespace for all subsequent kubectl commands in that context. kubectl config set-context --current --namespace = ggckad-s2
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Kubectl context and configuration”

notes.front: What is the kubectl shorthand for --all-namespaces?
notes.explanation: The Quick Reference points it out because appending --all-namespaces happens so often.
notes.evidence: Appending --all-namespaces happens frequently enough that you should be aware of the shorthand for --all-namespaces : kubectl -A
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “A note on --all-namespaces”

notes.front: After alias k=kubectl, which line makes bash completion work for k too?
notes.explanation: The Quick Reference pairs the alias with this line so that the shorthand keeps completion.
notes.evidence: You can also use a shorthand alias for kubectl that also works with completion: alias k = kubectl complete -o default -F __start_kubectl k
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Kubectl autocomplete”

notes.front: What does kubectl set image deployment/frontend www=image:v2 do?
notes.back: Rolls out a new image to the “www” containers of Deployment frontend.
notes.explanation: The Quick Reference calls this a rolling update of those containers.
notes.evidence: kubectl set image deployment/frontend www = image:v2 # Rolling update "www" containers of "frontend" deployment, updating the image
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Updating resources”

notes.front: Deployment api runs container app on image shop:1.4. You must move it to shop:1.5 with a rolling update and no file edits. Which command?
notes.choices:
A) kubectl set image deployment/api app=shop:1.5
B) kubectl set image deployment/api shop:1.5
C) kubectl rollout restart deployment/api
notes.choicesExplained: B: set image needs container=image pairs; the container name is missing. C: a restart re-creates Pods on the same image.
notes.explanation: set image names the container and its new image, and the Deployment rolls the change out.
notes.evidence: kubectl set image deployment/frontend www = image:v2 # Rolling update "www" containers of "frontend" deployment, updating the image
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Updating resources”

notes.front: How do you remove the label new-label from Pod my-pod?
notes.back: kubectl label pods my-pod new-label- (a trailing minus).
notes.explanation: Without the minus, key=value in the same place adds a label instead.
notes.evidence: kubectl label pods my-pod new-label = awesome # Add a Label kubectl label pods my-pod new-label- # Remove a label
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Updating resources”

notes.front: Which flag must kubectl label have to change a label that already has a value?
notes.explanation: The Quick Reference uses it to overwrite an existing value, as distinct from adding a new label.
notes.evidence: kubectl label pods my-pod new-label = new-value --overwrite # Overwrite an existing value
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Updating resources”

notes.front: Node worker-2 carries disk=hdd. A task says it now has SSDs and must be labelled disk=ssd. Which command works?
notes.choices:
A) kubectl label node worker-2 disk=ssd --overwrite
B) kubectl label node worker-2 disk=ssd
C) kubectl annotate node worker-2 disk=ssd
notes.choicesExplained: B: the Quick Reference adds --overwrite exactly when an existing value is changed. C: annotate sets an annotation, a different kind of metadata from a label.
notes.explanation: Changing an existing label’s value is the overwrite case the Quick Reference shows.
notes.evidence: kubectl label pods my-pod new-label = new-value --overwrite # Overwrite an existing value
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Updating resources”

notes.front: Which command adds the annotation icon-url=http://example.com/i.png to Pod my-pod?
notes.explanation: kubectl annotate mirrors kubectl label, including the trailing minus to remove one.
notes.evidence: kubectl annotate pods my-pod icon-url = http://goo.gl/XXBTWq # Add an annotation kubectl annotate pods my-pod icon-url- # Remove annotation
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Updating resources”

notes.front: Which command scales ReplicaSet foo to three replicas?
notes.explanation: `scale` sets the replica count of the controller you name, written as type/name, so `rs/foo` is the ReplicaSet foo.
notes.evidence: kubectl scale --replicas = 3 rs/foo # Scale a replicaset named 'foo' to 3
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Scaling resources”

notes.front: Deployment web must run 6 Pods from now on. Which command does it in one step?
notes.choices:
A) kubectl scale deployment/web --replicas=6
B) kubectl autoscale deployment web --min=6
C) kubectl run web --replicas=6
notes.choicesExplained: B: autoscale creates an autoscaler that changes the count by itself; it is not a fixed count. C: kubectl run creates a single Pod, not a Deployment’s replica count.
notes.explanation: scale sets the controller’s replica count directly.
notes.evidence: scale : Horizontally scale a controller to add or remove Pods by updating the replica count of the controller.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to update objects”

notes.front: What does kubectl edit do?
notes.back: Opens a live object’s raw configuration in an editor so you can change it directly.
notes.explanation: Like patch, it needs a better grasp of the object schema than the verb-driven update commands.
notes.evidence: The kubectl tool supports these additional ways to update a live object directly, however they require a better understanding of the Kubernetes object schema. edit : Directly edit the raw configuration of a live object by opening its configuration in an editor.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to update objects”

notes.front: You must change one probe setting on a running Deployment and see its full spec while doing it. Which command fits?
notes.choices:
A) kubectl edit deployment/<name>
B) kubectl set image deployment/<name>
C) kubectl scale deployment/<name>
notes.choicesExplained: B: set image changes only container images. C: scale changes only the replica count.
notes.explanation: edit opens the live object’s whole configuration in an editor, so any field can be changed.
notes.evidence: edit : Directly edit the raw configuration of a live object by opening its configuration in an editor.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to update objects”

notes.front: What does kubectl patch do?
notes.back: Changes specific fields of a live object, given as a patch string.
notes.explanation: Only the fields named in the patch string change.
notes.evidence: patch : Directly modify specific fields of a live object by using a patch string.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to update objects”

notes.front: What does kubectl replace --force do, and what is the cost?
notes.back: It deletes and then re-creates the resource, which causes a service outage.
notes.explanation: Because the object is deleted first, it is gone until the new one is created.
notes.evidence: Force replace, delete and then re-create the resource. Will cause a service outage. kubectl replace --force -f ./pod.json
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Updating resources”

notes.front: How is kubectl delete used as an imperative command rather than with a configuration file?
notes.back: You pass the object as an argument, e.g. kubectl delete deployment/nginx.
notes.explanation: The same command serves both styles; only the arguments differ.
notes.evidence: The difference is in the arguments passed to the command. To use kubectl delete as an imperative command, pass the object to be deleted as an argument.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to delete objects”

notes.front: kubectl get against kubectl describe: what does each print?
notes.back: get: basic information about matching objects. describe: aggregated, detailed information about them.
notes.explanation: Both are viewing commands; logs is the third, printing a container’s stdout and stderr.
notes.evidence: get : Prints basic information about matching objects. Use get -h to see a list of options. describe : Prints aggregated detailed information about matching objects. logs : Prints the stdout and stderr for a container running in a Pod.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “Managing Kubernetes Objects Using Imperative Commands”, “How to view an object”

notes.front: Which kubectl output format adds extra columns and, for Pods, the node name?
notes.explanation: It stays plain text, just with additional information.
notes.evidence: -o=wide Output in the plain-text format with any additional information, and for pods, the node name is included
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Formatting output”

notes.front: Which kubectl output format prints only the resource name and nothing else?
notes.explanation: Every other column, such as status and age, is left out.
notes.evidence: -o=name Print only the resource name and nothing else
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Formatting output”

notes.front: Which kubectl output format prints a table from a comma-separated list of columns you define?
notes.explanation: The spec is a comma-separated list, one entry per column.
notes.evidence: -o=custom-columns=<spec> Print a table using a comma separated list of custom columns
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Formatting output”

notes.front: A task wants the names of all Deployments in a namespace written to a file, one per line, with no headers or other columns. Which output fits best?
notes.choices:
A) -o name
B) -o wide
C) -o yaml
notes.choicesExplained: B: wide adds columns rather than removing them. C: yaml prints the whole object, not just its name.
notes.explanation: The name format prints only the resource name and nothing else.
notes.evidence: -o=name Print only the resource name and nothing else
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Formatting output”

notes.front: In kubectl JSONPath output, what encloses each JSONPath expression?
notes.explanation: kubectl uses the expressions to pick fields out of the JSON object and format the output.
notes.evidence: A JSONPath template is composed of JSONPath expressions enclosed by curly braces: { and } . Kubectl uses JSONPath expressions to filter on specific fields in the JSON object and format the output.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “JSONPath Support”, “JSONPath Support”

notes.front: Which JSONPath operators does kubectl add for iterating over a list?
notes.explanation: The docs’ examples wrap the per-item fields between {range .items[*]} and {end}.
notes.evidence: Use the range , end operators to iterate lists.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “JSONPath Support”, “JSONPath Support”

notes.front: Can kubectl JSONPath filters match with regular expressions?
notes.back: No. Use a tool such as jq on -o json output instead.
notes.explanation: The docs show a =~ filter that does not work, and a jq select with test() that does.
notes.evidence: JSONPath regular expressions are not supported. If you want to match using regular expressions, you can use a tool such as jq .
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “JSONPath Support”, “Regular expressions in JSONPath”

notes.front: Complete the command that prints all nodes’ external IPs: kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.addresses[{{c1::?(@.type=="ExternalIP")}}].address}'
notes.explanation: The ?() filter keeps only the addresses whose type is ExternalIP.
notes.evidence: Get ExternalIPs of all nodes kubectl get nodes -o jsonpath = '{.items[*].status.addresses[?(@.type=="ExternalIP")].address}'
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Viewing and finding resources”

notes.front: A script needs just the images used by the Pods matching app=api, space-separated, with no table. Which output fits?
notes.choicesExplained: B: wide prints a table with more columns, not bare images. C: name prints the Pod names, not their images.
notes.explanation: JSONPath picks exactly the fields you name out of the JSON object, as in the Quick Reference’s version-label example.
notes.evidence: Get the version label of all pods with label app=cassandra kubectl get pods --selector = app = cassandra -o \ jsonpath = '{.items[*].metadata.labels.version}'
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Viewing and finding resources”

notes.front: Complete the command that lists Pods by restart count: kubectl get pods --sort-by={{c1::'.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount'}}
notes.explanation: --sort-by takes a field path into each object.
notes.evidence: List pods Sorted by Restart Count kubectl get pods --sort-by = '.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount'
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Viewing and finding resources”

notes.front: How do you set kubectl’s log verbosity?
notes.back: With -v or --v followed by an integer log level.
notes.explanation: The levels follow the general Kubernetes logging conventions.
notes.evidence: Kubectl verbosity is controlled with the -v or --v flags followed by an integer representing the log level. General Kubernetes logging conventions and the associated log levels are described here
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, “kubectl Quick Reference”, “Kubectl output verbosity and debugging”

notes.front: In the exam, where must you do each task?
notes.back: On the task’s designated host, reached with the ssh command from the base system.
notes.explanation: The instructions at the top of each task tell you which host to connect to, and you exit back to the base machine when done.
notes.source: Linux Foundation, “Important Instructions: CKA and CKAD”, “CKA and CKAD Exam Environment”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Why will kubectl not work on the exam’s base system (hostname base)?
notes.back: The base system has none of the exam tools installed; all tasks are meant for the designated hosts.
notes.explanation: The Linux Foundation installs the tools only where the tasks are done, the designated hosts.
notes.source: Linux Foundation, “Important Instructions: CKA and CKAD”, “CKA and CKAD Exam Environment”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: You finish task 3 on host node-a, and task 4 names host node-b. What do you do?
notes.back: Exit the ssh session back to base, then ssh to node-b.
notes.choices:
A) exit to base, then ssh node-b
B) ssh node-b from inside node-a
C) Stay on node-a and run the task with --context
notes.choicesExplained: B: nested ssh sessions are not supported in the exam. C: each task must be done on its own designated host.
notes.explanation: The exam expects one hop from base to each task’s host and back.
notes.source: Linux Foundation, “Important Instructions: CKA and CKAD”, “CKA and CKAD Exam Environment”
